notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg2200.tlg00536.opp-gr: 1.1: <τι> is an editorial supplement. 9.1: 'σιγᾷς ἄκων ἑκὼν οὐ σωφρονήσας' read as an antithesis (unwilling silence for not being prudent willingly). 11.1: 'ἐξανάλωτο' taken as pluperfect 'had been used up'.

Scanning errors corrected: '(5 βέλτιστε' read as ὦ βέλτιστε (21); 'τοξότ’ ἃς' as τοξότας (21); 'ἐξουσέας' as ἐξουσίας (30). In 36 the speech shifts to the first person, apparently an imagined utterance of the mutilated orator; quotation marks added for clarity. The final clause of 17 ('ἐδόκει τῷ πλουσίῳ, καὶ ἀπηλλάττοντο') is elliptical; rendered literally.

37: χειρῶν παλαιστήν read as χειρῶν παλαιστήν (depriving a wrestler of his hands); construction elliptical. 41: παρῄ εἰν read as παρῄειν. 43: οἶ read as οἱ. 46: τυραννίδος ὠμότητα παρελθών taken as 'surpassed'; ἐπὶ τοῖς νόμοις εὐπορῶν ('well supplied against the laws') is uncertain. 48: φανεὶς τρέπεσθαι is elliptical; object '[the enemy]' supplied.

55: 'the gift' (τὴν δωρεάν) apparently refers to the people's grant of the tongue to the rich man in return for his raising the siege; 'the stones' in 56 presumably alludes to an earlier episode in the declamation (perhaps the crowd stoning or pelting the rich man's party), not recoverable from this stretch.

nodes.text: XXXVI.

A law: the one responsible for uproar and civil strife is to die. A poor orator was the political enemy of a rich man. During a famine and a siege the rich man promised victory, if the poor man's tongue were cut out. He got [it]. Going out by night, he drove off the enemy. On the day he was addressing the people, the poor man, who was present, wept. The people stoned the rich man, and the poor man is charged under the law.
Defence speech of an orator.

The man who has spoken much from this platform, judges, often either prosecuting wrongdoers or helping those wronged, stands silent now, holding his hope of safety in the tongues of others; and we who still have some voice left, and the rich, must contend alongside [him] with all that is in us, and not stand by while the strength of justice is harmed by the defendant's speechlessness, not only because it is fitting everywhere to take forethought for this side and for those outside misfortune to defend the helpless, but because this very man, who now looks to us, often stood beside us too when we were maliciously prosecuted, and helped to save us.

And we would be the worst of all men if we failed to repay [him] at so pressing a moment; and it is right that you too, judges, out of respect for justice and pity for his suffering, should not add to the poor man a greater evil: to seem to have broken a law.

The poor man himself, then, does not fear death, but would very much wish to depart; for one who won repute from speaking and had his public life as consolation for his poverty, and then has been robbed of the ability to give counsel, would count his end a gain. Yet it does not befit you, because living is a burden to the accused, to vote death against him. For a man who is unjustly a defendant before you, but who through having met with misfortune desires his end, must be saved by you, and afterwards deliberate with himself about this. For the vote, I think, should be cast not according to the desires of the litigants, but according to justice.

I do not know, judges, what this wretched man must become in order to escape the abuse of the wealthy. For when he used speech on your behalf, he was robbed of his tongue by his enemies, as one who would cause no more trouble; and again, having fallen silent, he is tried as a wrongdoer. But if both speaking and not speaking he is to be under accusations and in trouble, what must he seek to obtain security?

So for those who suffer terribly on every side and are not allowed even to breathe, the one refuge is your humanity, judges. It is right that this man too should now enjoy it, especially since in appearance the poor man is on trial, but in truth the people are being tested. For the deed concerning the rich man was theirs, so that the people must share with the defendant in the vote, whichever way it goes.

Let none of you think of [the rich man] as a benefactor struck down by stones, nor be led on by the praises which the prosecutor went through in glorifying the rich man, dramatising the siege, marvelling at the strange sortie, and extolling the speed of the victory. For if you receive our speech too in calm, I think I shall show that he was not only no benefactor, but even malicious toward you, and had contrived the war, rather than resolving dangers that arose of themselves.

7. But allow me, judges, first to speak briefly to the poor man. For this is what remains for him: to hear others speaking. Your political career has brought you to this, unhappy man. Not recognising fortune has led you to this pitch of misfortune. From your noble decrees this dreadful thing grew for you, from beneficial laws, from democratic freedom of speech.

It was splendid to state the best opinion, to persuade [the people] to what was needed, and to prevent improper things being done; splendid, but perilous. It was just to labour together with your country, to care for its freedom, and to expose a scheming rich man; just, but not safe. You trusted in the laws for help. Did you not know, then, that laws too are often defeated by money? Did you not hear the poets singing of the power of wealth, and how it leads human affairs wherever it wishes?

But did you hope to overcome riches by just means, you, to overcome wealth, a man who barely owns a rotten cloak? Was it not better to think more modestly, collect silver, and build up your house? But, you busybody who do not know yourself, you clashed with, hated, provoked a man who could very easily have acquired even a tyranny. Therefore you have been punished in your voice, through which you caused offence, and you are silent against your will, since you were not prudent by your will.

For since, judges, though he turned everything over and left no attempt untried, he could neither catch this man through malicious prosecution, nor win him over with money and persuade him to become one of the hirelings around him, and he wanted to break the laws, but this man would not let him, he saw that while the city was in good cheer it was impossible to get satisfaction from the poor man, but that he must bring danger and set it over the commonwealth, and drive affairs into such narrow straits of hope that the people would yield everything and disregard the laws in their fear.

What then does he attempt? See how cleverly he brings a war into the country and sets an army moving against us. It was surely not hard, by spending gold on generals and taxiarchs and promising to help in other matters, to persuade them to take up arms. When, then, the war fell suddenly upon the country, we, as befitted good men, were thinking of going out, preventing, repelling, such things; but he, putting on the air of one who was afraid and distressed at the situation, took over the platform and held the people back with long speeches, now saying that the matter needed much deliberation, now explaining that the attackers' force was irresistible, and the next day similar things, and again much the same. And they were approaching the wall, while we were listening to speeches; the man who spoke against him was muzzled, and the grain had been used up.

And when that noble man perceived that we had come to the extremity of despair, and thought that his plan was now reaching its goal, he who with us and before us had trembled and shrunk, suddenly bold and brave, from the luxury you know of, says, 'What do you want? That the siege be lifted? I grant you this. I preside over the victory. It is in my power that the city be troubled no longer. But I must first receive a gift.'

We agreed, and he, turning to his request, what a voice, what a voice, O Sun, did he let out! The guardian of persons and of laws, promising even a trophy, did not ask for plethra of land, nor public maintenance, nor to stand [as a statue] in bronze, those customary rewards of democracy. It would have been moderate if he had asked for the poor man's death. For even if very cruel and savage, at least the departed have no perception of what they have suffered. But not even this was enough for him; but, O gods and spirits, oh, what novel punishment! he went for the tongue of one of the citizens. He asked as the prize for his valour the orator's speechlessness, mixing the cruelty of tyranny with the form of democracy. The gift was a decree, but the audacity was tyrannical. And he asked to receive from us as though there were laws, but sought to receive what is forbidden by the laws.

So the people, when they heard, were struck by the word, and we looked at one another, hating the request, but pained by the siege, and we were at a loss, caught between a monstrous gift and a hard crisis; and while we hesitated, this great-souled man, who lived for public life, though able to speak against [it], chose to keep quiet, and offered himself very resolutely to the cutting, and, lacking money, contributed his tongue to us.

When the fine gift had now been fulfilled, we waited for the victory and considered what the manner of it would be. Will he go out taking the hoplites? Or will he rely on the archers for the task? Will he set an ambush? What so great thing has he found with which to overawe an army elated by its successes? So we [thought]; but he strolled at ease within the walls until evening itself, and when it was already midnight, he crossed beyond the gates and met with the enemy, and they went away as though a general had ordered it.

Does this not shout, does this not cry aloud that the whole thing had been arranged and managed by the rich man, and that they came and went away again according to his will? For on reflection I cannot see how I could call this a victory. Does one man, defeated, drive off a victorious army, shut in, a besieging one? A rich man drives off an army, a soft-living, effeminate, enervated man, who has neither practised nor learned anything straightforward or noble, but has spent his life in contentiousness and pettiness?

And while of the rest of you, so many as you are and diligently practising warfare from boyhood, none saw this, that one must attack by night, nor dared [to], did the money-maker, a man whose whole zeal lies in that direction, like some divine power, turn the besiegers' blockade into flight? It is not so. No, the enemy had to sit before [the city] until the poor man's disaster, and when he had suffered what he has suffered, the rich man saw fit, and they departed.

But I leave this aside, lest I seem to some to be speaking off the subject. As for what followed, then: he called everyone to an assembly, preening himself on his splendid victory, and as many came running together, this orator too went along to see the gathering. When he saw you and you saw him, he wept, and you pitied [him], and, taking to mind what sort of gift you had given, you exacted justice for what had been forced [on you].

Then I beheld a lawful assembly, a free people, a stoning befitting our constitution. The man fell upon the platform who had disgraced the platform with his decree. You made a fine defence to the Greeks with your stones; you finely undid the disgrace incurred under compulsion by the deeds done in freedom from fear. You showed that the vote was the crisis's, not [an expression] of the city's character.

20. So we congratulate one another on our spirit and our just anger, and live on believing we have done the holiest thing of all; but for the poor man the misfortune does not stop: he is brought to court and tried, and is charged with breaking the law on riot and civil strife. For this is what remains: that the guardian of the laws be ranked among the lawbreakers.

And by saying what, my good sir, did he cause the riot? Did he propose confiscating the property of some of the rich, and strife broke out? Did he propose that the poor keep silent, and so create strife? Did he set the hoplites against the cavalry, the archers against the slingers, the generals against the taxiarchs, slandering each in turn? By what decree did he divide the city? By what proposal did he split the people?

Are you not ashamed, by Zeus, to accuse a voiceless man of riot, just as if someone were to accuse this very man of supplying the enemy? You fool, the wretched man's concern is with his bare sustenance. So you too, look at the orator's tongue and stop your accusations. As it is, you are doing almost the same as if you were to blame the statues too for causing a riot among the people.

It is against those who speak, you sycophant, and take part in public life and propose measures, that such accusations lie, and it is to such men that the law addresses itself, suspicious of the counsels of some. For a harmful speech persuasively composed naturally robs the hearers of their reasoning, and persuades them to think harmful things useful and useful things damaging. In this way a city is driven to war against itself and a people carried away into strife. And then the one who supplied the impulse must be answerable for what is done by the people. For what would not have been done had the words not been spoken, this, having been done because of the words, recoils upon the one who spoke them. How then is one who has no share in speech responsible for things that belong to speakers alone? Did this man, who now contends through others, throw the people into turmoil, he who is silent, he who does not open his mouth?

24. And where is it even fitting to call what was done 'strife'? The people took vengeance for a wicked gift, using a single mind in [taking up] the stones, of one accord, provoked in common. And there was no riot, with some planning one thing and others another; rather, all hated [him] and stoned [him].

Strife is when difference of desire sets people in turmoil against each other, when, split in their opinions, some seize the heights and others hold the harbours, when they build walls across [the city], when they call in allies against one another, when the city does not remain one. But to take vengeance on an inhuman man, what riot is that, or what sort of strife?

26. But grant that what happened concerning the rich man was both riot and strife. Yet this man at least is not the cause. For who heard him saying: 'Strike, citizens, the tyrant's head. Strike the rich man who trampled on us in our crisis. The dangers are past. Exact justice'? He said none of this; nor could he have, had he wished. How then, by the gods, is he brought under the law for his silence?

If, while this man was silent, another, using these words, had moved the people to the deed, would they not have turned the charge against that man, insisting on the words? So by the very [argument] by which they would have tried the speaker, by this they acquit the one who did not utter a sound.

28. 'But he came,' he says, 'to the assembly.' And what law has forbidden it? 'And standing there he wept.' And where is lamenting a crime? An unfortunate citizen took part in the assembly in tears. Trials for such things I do not know of, neither held among us nor among our neighbours, neither in the time of us still living nor in that of our ancestors. Rather, it is permitted to smile and it is granted to weep, and one cannot demand that nature render account. Just as by breathing, being hungry, rejoicing, laughing, scowling, being ill and suffering such things one cannot do wrong, so too one cannot be liable to trial for lamenting and weeping.

Do you see those who follow the dead to their tombs? They weep, but they are not tried. Do you see those who are cut by doctors? They cry out, but are not charged. How many orators, recalling allies who have met misfortune, shed tears along with their words; how many peoples, hearing of the disasters of their colonists, have been brought down to lamentation! If, then, you count weeping among crimes at all, you are failing to prosecute many wrongdoers; but if in the case of others the thing is not answerable, you are being officious in the present case.

Tell me: are you above grief at your sufferings, or, if you grieved and were then made to pay a penalty, would you accept it? No, you neither overcome nature in that way nor are you without feeling. Do not, then, deprive another of the liberty you yourself think fit to enjoy. And in general, you did not come in to make law, but to follow those laid down long ago. Show, then, tears counted among the crimes in the laws in force.

For we distinguish wrongdoers from those who are not by this: that the former dare what is forbidden, the latter do what is allowed. For instance, we bring the thief, the adulterer and the murderer to court. Why? Because they do what has been written must not be done. The man who chatters, walks, moves his hands, shouts, and screws up his face we do not bring in or try. Why? Because they do not break laws.

So you too must show this written down: 'If anyone weeps, let him be punished like those who commit other crimes.' If you cannot, you are acting out of spite and making habitual sycophants more dangerous, training them and teaching them to make anything that turns up a pretext for an indictment.

33. But if not in the laws, show it specified in the decree of the gift: 'Let the poor man not appear at the assembly, nor bewail his suffering, nor grieve at his disaster.' But not even the hostile man, who shrank from nothing, deprived him of these. You, though, show yourself harsher to us than the rich man.

Further, if, while unharmed and having nothing to groan about, he had wept on purpose to stir up the people, I would myself have blamed him, I would myself have indicted him. As it is, even if he tried very hard, it would not be easy not to lament; rather, the suffering lodged in his tongue sets the flow of tears moving. For surely the orator cannot take refuge in an example and find relief from similar cases?

He has not lost a child, he has not been condemned to disenfranchisement, the things that befall many; he did not have his hand cut off by a decree of the people, so that he could console his suffering with his tongue; but that by which we differ from the irrational animals, the use of speech with one another, this he has lost for another's pleasure. And now he stands voiceless, like men of stone, he who until lately flowed [with words] on the platform. What should one even call the man? His art bids [us call him] an orator, but his tongue does not allow it.

No more pitiable suffering has occurred in all of time. 'Zealous on the people's behalf, I am punished; benefiting the community with my voice, I am deprived of my voice; and silence becomes my reward for goodwill, and I have my tongue cut out at the command of a rich enemy. For everything, even the smallest thing, is unbearable to me when the one causing the pain is hostile; but punished in my tongue, what shall I do?'

Add, then, the orator too. For in this respect he differs most of all. For the orator is nothing other than voice. And for such a man it is a lighter misfortune to lack his eyes than his tongue. For a private citizen will perhaps bear it moderately, since he has not acquired his good repute through his voice; but to deprive an orator of his tongue is the same as [depriving] a wrestler of his hands.

Are you surprised, then, if a voiceless orator weeps? Do you think his life is anything other than weeping? At home he laments, using a nod for every need. In the marketplace he laments, unable to address his acquaintances. And what wonder is it that the sufferer weeps, if we ourselves fall to tears at the sight of the orator?

He wept longing for his voice. What is new in that? Everyone uses what he has freely, but this man cannot rejoice [in it]. For even if he had not wept before, would not the assembly have stirred his lamentation? The orator saw his old darlings, the platform and the presiding officers, the councillors and the people, the chairman and the prytaneis; he saw his enemy raising his hand, he heard him declaiming, he heard the herald crying out: 'Who wishes to speak?' And seeking his voice he did not find it. So he set his present silence against his former oratory, and saw his own misfortune more clearly in the rich man's public speech; and, looking upon the posture in which he himself once took pride, he was struck to the soul by the memory of former times.

If you maimed a runner's leg and then brought him to watch a race, seeing the racecourse and his leg together he will shed many tears. If you cut off a noble general's right hand and brought him to see a battle, setting the absence of his hand beside the work of the spears, he will not bear the sight without tears. And if you ruined a painter's fingers and showed him a painting, he will fall to lamenting at the memory of his art. For a place, an object and an action can all recall former good fortune, and this brings on tears.

So too the tongueless orator saw an assembly and remembered the affairs of the time when he had his voice. Surely he reflected somehow to himself: 'Once I came forward here, and I went up onto the platform, and I made proposals, and I was applauded, and through me the city did most of its business; but now I stand like a statue, a witness of others' good things.' Look, you too, jurors, are weeping. What, then, was it likely that this man would feel?

But if he did not weep for himself, but, having found a beneficial proposal and then being unable to speak it, wept for the city, for what advisers it has been deprived of, does he for this reason owe the city a penalty? And for what do you demand punishment? If for the tears, it was permitted to weep; if because he stirred the people, he was no prophet, nor did he foresee what was to come. And there are no penalties for ignorance. For who has been punished because he did not foresee what would happen? But you, if you knew of the anger that would come, why did you not drive him away as quickly as possible, before the people did anything? And if you did not foresee it, why do you exact a penalty rather than pay one?

But you have not escaped notice: you have made this man your pretext, while accusing the people. And what do I say? The people were going to do just what they did, even if no poor man had either come or wept. For those who are forced to give what they do not wish to give, once they come into power over what they unwillingly surrendered, exact punishment out of the very things they gave, making war on the one who received them. For what fortune of war, what grievous crisis forced such a decree to be ratified in the city: 'Let a citizen's tongue be cut out'? Why? Because, possessing little, he opposes the rich man in politics.

By this decree, jurors, democracy was being dissolved, and laws and sacred and holy things were being dissolved; the earth was being defiled, and the sun that oversees all things; the established order was being thrown into confusion, and the noble thing that is equal freedom of speech was being turned into despotism; the city was being filled with pollution, and you were sharing in the cruelty by your show of hands. It was clear, then, that once affairs had settled, the season of calm would be a season of punishment for the rich man too; and the people's judgement coincided with the poor man's tears.

So you did no wrong, jurors, in then using stones against a man who had revelled in your misfortunes; indeed, you would not have wiped away the disgrace if you had not snatched up the stones. For how could you have gone into the temples? How could you have sacrificed? How could you have held the festivals in full? How could you have asked good things from the gods while the rich man laid his polluted hand on the sacred things alongside you? And who, called on as an ally, would have answered the call to share in your actions?

Do you not know that the characters of cities are recognised by their decrees, and are judged according to the virtue or vice of those decrees? What sort of men in your ways would you have been thought, had you stood by the gift and not purified yourselves by the killing? I, for my part, think: more savage than the barbarians. But now it has been shown to all that the gift was not, after all, the city's, and the earlier acts are overshadowed by the later. The man has fallen who in a free state surpassed the cruelty of a tyranny. The man has fallen who learned to overstep the customs of democracy. A rich man was stoned who was well supplied against the laws. And then does anyone resent his end, and indict and prosecute?

I fear, jurors, the accuser: he grieves for a dead tyrant. And yet, was he throwing stones with you or not? If he took part in the throwing, how does he accuse what he himself did? But if he alone held back, he had condemned the people of madness.

But if you speak to me of the night and the victory, you speak of a trick, you speak of a deception, you speak of the work of money. For if he was so strong that he put [the enemy] to flight by appearing, and alone was more powerful than the whole city, the report of his courage would not have escaped the enemy, nor would they have marched against a city in which such a soldier was reared; no, that man has paid the penalty for two things: the siege which he contrived and the gift which he requested.

But you, jurors, do not renew with your vote the shame that came from the decree, nor kill the wronged man as a wrongdoer, nor convict the stoning by your verdict. The law speaks of the cause of riot and strife. But he is not the cause, for he was silent. Coming into the assembly he wept. But both of these are permitted. He was compelled by his suffering to weep. He did not know what would happen.

Save, then, jurors, the man who is the victim of a sycophant, who has done no wrong at all but has suffered things most unheard-of. Surely if even some foreigner had come to such misfortunes, you would certainly have pitied him on seeing him. And this gathering is a token of your humanity.

That popular orator, who vexed the rich on behalf of the laws, who spoke many proposals, wrote many decrees, undertook many embassies, who won over allies, who found revenues, who enacted good laws and repealed bad ones, who presided over many affairs yet remained in poverty, this man to whom we looked in our needs, repay now to the unfortunate the favour by saving him, and do not make it plain that those who serve your interests are out of their minds.

For whom of all men will you help, if you do not pity this one? Toward whom will you be compassionate, if you neglect this man? You could find no man more well-disposed nor more wretched, who has even confirmed the absurdities of myths by his own sufferings. The rich man took him and led him from the assembly, and he followed like a captive. And surrounding him with his flatterers, reminding him of his free speech and displaying the decree, he said, 'Put out, then, the tongue that is hostile to me, the popular one, the one that did not fear wealth, the one stronger than fortune.' And the one gave the order, the other submitted, and the voice that kept the city's affairs upright was cut out.

Will you then add a further condemnation to the man who has suffered such things, and to one for whom no consolation can be found, will you add misfortunes? And will you be harming this man, or the community? The decree about the tongue, jurors, has sufficiently cowed the poor, has sufficiently shown that the post of goodwill is dangerous. And if they should also see this man condemned in a court, when will they give themselves eagerly to your affairs? Who will speak? Who will serve as envoy? Who will be just, seeing such prizes set out for justice?

Shall some, then, change sides and think it good counsel to stand together with the rich, while others have licence to overrun the constitution? These things destroy democracy, these things bring in oligarchy. From such seeds slavery grows for a people. In this one body, then, the community shares the danger.

55. But you, come up here for me and contribute something. You have hands, you have tears. You do not lack the means for supplication. And if these are not enough, show your tongue. Do you see how the jurors have been moved? Take heart, then, about the vote, and do not blame the people. Groaning, it voted the gift, overcome by the crisis. Many men have often given themselves up to slaughter for their countries. You too, by the cutting, ended the siege. Among your benefactions I shall also inscribe your suffering.

So forget the decree, but remember that fine assembly and the stones. Keep for me your old resolve and guard your principles, I beg you, even in silence toward public affairs. Write counsels. I shall read them out, and if I find some proposal, I shall share it with you. And you shake your head and nod, and take part in politics by your nods. Compose a defence on behalf of the people, for it befits you, even having suffered, to bring credit to the city; compose an exhortation to the poor to be eager, take away their fear, strengthen them toward goodwill. And the city will maintain you at public expense, consoling an orator who is both voiceless and poor.
